questions.q: Your tower of blocks falls down. You feel cross. What can you do first?
o: Say you will never play again
questions.why: Slow breaths calm your body, so you can build again with a clear head.

questions.q: Your friend Tara is crying in the playground. What should you do?
o: Sit with her and ask, "Are you okay?"
questions.why: Asking gently shows you care, and it helps her feel less alone.

questions.q: You feel butterflies in your tummy before your dance show. What is this feeling?
questions.why: Butterflies in the tummy often mean we are a little nervous. It is normal.

questions.q: Kabir won't share the swing. You feel upset. What is a good thing to say?
o: "Can I have a turn after you?"
"I will tell everyone you are bad."
questions.why: Asking for a turn uses calm words and keeps everyone safe.

questions.q: You made a card for Nani and she smiled. How do you feel?
questions.why: Making someone smile usually gives us a warm, happy feeling.

questions.q: You broke Mumma's cup by mistake. What is the best thing to do?
o: Tell her the truth and say sorry
Hide the pieces under the sofa
Run to your room and say nothing
questions.why: Telling the truth is brave, and saying sorry helps fix things.

questions.q: Your friend got a new bicycle and you feel a little jealous. What helps?
o: Say "It's lovely!" and remember your own good things
Tell your friend it is ugly
questions.why: Being happy for a friend while remembering what you have helps the jealous feeling pass.

questions.q: You are angry and want to hit someone. What can you do instead?
o: Walk away and squeeze a soft pillow
questions.why: Moving away and squeezing something soft lets the anger out without hurting anyone.

questions.q: A new girl, Diya, sits alone at lunch. How might she feel?
questions.why: Sitting alone in a new place can make someone feel lonely.

questions.q: You lost the running race. What can you say to yourself?
o: "I tried my best. I'll practise more."
questions.why: Kind words to yourself help you feel better and try again.

questions.q: Your little sister is scared of the thunder. What can you do?
o: Hold her hand and say, "It's just a loud noise."
Tell her the house will fall
questions.why: Comforting words help scared people feel safe.

questions.q: You feel very sad because your goldfish died. What helps?
o: Talk to Papa about how you feel
Say you don't care at all
questions.why: Sharing sad feelings with someone you trust makes them easier to carry.

questions.q: Your friend Arjun says, "I don't want to play now." What should you do?
o: Grab his arm and pull him
Tell him you will never play with him again
questions.why: Everyone can say no sometimes. Respecting it keeps the friendship strong.

questions.q: You are excited about your birthday and keep jumping in class. What is a good idea?
o: Save the jumping for break time
Pull your friend's hair for fun
questions.why: Feeling excited is great, and waiting for the right time is kind to others.

questions.q: Your face is hot and your hands are fists. What feeling might this be?
questions.why: A hot face and tight fists are signs of anger in the body.

questions.q: Your teacher says your drawing is messy. You feel hurt. What can you do?
o: Ask, "How can I make it neater?"
questions.why: Asking how to improve turns a hurt feeling into learning.

questions.q: You see a boy fall and scrape his knee. What should you do?
o: Help him up and call a teacher
questions.why: Helping someone who is hurt shows kindness.

questions.q: You don't want to go to school because you feel worried. What helps?
o: Tell Mumma or Papa what is worrying you
Pretend to be sick every day
questions.why: Talking about worries helps grown-ups help you.

questions.q: Your best friend is playing with someone else today. How can you feel better?
o: Tell the other child to go away
Say you are not friends any more
questions.why: Friends can have many friends. Playing together makes everyone happy.

questions.q: You finished a hard puzzle all by yourself! What feeling is this?
questions.why: Doing something hard by yourself makes us feel proud.

questions.q: Mumma looks tired after work. What is a kind thing to do?
o: Bring her a glass of water
Ask her to play loud games right away
Make a big mess to clean
questions.why: Noticing someone is tired and helping is very kind.

questions.q: Your cousin pulled your hair. You are really angry. What should you say?
questions.why: Using strong, clear words tells others how you feel without hurting them.

questions.q: You are scared of the dark at night. What can you do?
o: Tell Papa and ask for a small night light
questions.why: Telling a grown-up helps you find a way to feel safe.

questions.q: Your friend says, "I got a gold star!" How can you show you care?
questions.why: Cheering for friends makes them feel happy and makes you a good friend.

questions.q: You feel a little lonely at home. What can you do?
o: Ask Dadi to read a story with you
Stay alone in a dark room
questions.why: Asking someone to spend time with you is a good way to feel less lonely.

questions.q: You spilled paint on Neel's picture by mistake. He is sad. What do you do?
o: Say sorry and offer to help fix it
questions.why: Saying sorry and helping shows you understand how he feels.

questions.q: You are waiting for your turn on the slide. You feel impatient. What helps?
o: Count slowly to ten while you wait
questions.why: Counting slowly helps you wait calmly.

questions.q: Your grandfather is unwell. You feel worried. What can you do?
o: Hide in your room all day
Pretend he is fine and say nothing
questions.why: Doing something kind can help with worried feelings and cheers him up.

questions.q: A child calls you a name. You feel hurt. What is a good step?
questions.why: A teacher can help, and the mean name does not say who you really are.

questions.q: Your friend Zoya's kite got stuck in the tree. She looks upset. What can you say?
o: "Let's ask a grown-up to help get it."
questions.why: Offering help shows you understand her feelings.

questions.q: You feel happy and silly. Your class is in a quiet test. What do you do?
o: Tickle the friend next to you
questions.why: Good feelings are great, and waiting for the right time is respectful.

questions.q: You want the last laddoo but your brother wants it too. What is fair?
o: Lick it so he won't want it
questions.why: Sharing is fair and keeps everyone happy.

questions.q: You were told off for something you didn't do. You feel upset. What should you do?
o: Shout "It's not fair!" again and again
questions.why: Calm words help grown-ups understand the truth.

questions.q: Your pet dog is wagging its tail and jumping. How is it feeling?
questions.why: A wagging tail and jumping usually mean a dog is happy.

questions.q: You can't tie your shoelaces and you feel frustrated. What helps?
o: Take a break, then try again slowly
questions.why: Taking a break and trying again helps when something is hard.

questions.q: Your friend forgot your birthday. You feel sad. What is a good idea?
o: Tell them kindly, "Today is my birthday!"
questions.why: Telling friends kindly helps them understand, and they can still wish you.

questions.q: You see your mother smiling while reading a letter. How might she feel?
questions.why: A smile usually means someone is happy.

questions.q: You are nervous to read aloud in class. What can you do?
o: Take a deep breath and read slowly
Read as fast as you can and mumble
questions.why: A deep breath and reading slowly helps your voice feel steady.

questions.q: Your sister drew on your notebook. You are angry. What do you do?
o: Tell her, "Please don't draw on my things."
questions.why: Telling her calmly what you need is better than hurting her.

questions.q: You feel grumpy because you are hungry. What can you do?
o: Eat a healthy snack and then play
questions.why: Sometimes grumpiness comes from hunger. Eating helps you feel better.

questions.q: Your friend lost her pencil box and looks worried. What can you do?
questions.why: Helping a worried friend shows you care.

questions.q: You built a sandcastle and the waves broke it. You feel sad. What can you think?
o: "Waves are mean, I hate the beach."
questions.why: Thinking of a new chance helps sad feelings pass.

questions.q: You and Vihaan both want the red crayon. What is a kind idea?
o: Hide it so no one gets it
questions.why: Taking turns is fair and kind.

questions.q: Your teacher praises you. How can you say thanks?
o: Tell your friends they are not good
questions.why: Saying thank you shows you value kind words.

questions.q: You feel shy at a new birthday party. What can you do?
o: Say hello to one child and ask their name
Hide behind the curtain the whole time
questions.why: Starting with one hello makes shyness easier.

questions.q: Your friend Ishaan fell asleep in the car and missed the zoo. He is sad. What can you say?
o: "I'll tell you all about the animals!"
"I saw everything and you saw nothing."
questions.why: Sharing helps a sad friend feel included.

questions.q: You feel cross because it is raining and you can't play outside. What helps?
o: Blame your mother for the rain
questions.why: Finding another fun thing helps when plans change.

questions.q: Your classmate Reyansh shares his tiffin with you. How might you feel?
questions.why: When someone shares with us, we feel thankful.

questions.q: You hurt your friend's feelings by mistake. How can you tell?
o: She looks sad and goes quiet
questions.why: A sad face and going quiet can show hurt feelings.

questions.q: You are very angry. Which is a safe way to calm down?
questions.why: Counting backwards gives your mind time to calm down.

questions.q: Your little brother is crying because his balloon flew away. What do you do?
o: Give him a hug and help him draw a balloon
Laugh and point at the sky
Pop your own balloon in front of him
questions.why: A hug and a fun idea comfort a sad child.

questions.q: You feel worried about a test tomorrow. What helps most?
o: Practise a little and tell Mumma you are worried
questions.why: Practising and sharing worries both help you feel ready.

questions.q: Saanvi is laughing at a joke you told. How does she feel?
questions.why: Laughing at a joke shows happiness.

questions.q: You see two friends fighting. What is a good thing to do?
questions.why: A teacher can help stop a fight safely.

questions.q: You got a gift you did not like. What is a kind thing to say?
o: Throw it in the bin in front of them
questions.why: Thanking someone for their thought is kind, even if the gift is not your favourite.

questions.q: Your tummy feels tight because you had a bad dream. What can you do?
questions.why: Sharing a bad dream with someone you trust helps you feel safe again.

questions.q: Your class is going on a picnic tomorrow! What feeling is this?
questions.why: Looking forward to something fun is called feeling excited.

questions.q: Your friend says, "I feel sad today." What should you do first?
o: Change the topic to your toys
questions.why: Listening first shows you care about their feelings.

questions.q: You knocked over Kiara's bottle by mistake. What do you say?
o: "Oops, sorry! Let me help clean it."
questions.why: Owning up and helping makes things right.

questions.q: You feel left out when others play a game you don't know. What can you do?
o: Ask, "Can you teach me how to play?"
Cry and tell them they are mean
questions.why: Asking to learn helps you join in.

questions.q: You score lower than you expected in a maths test. Which thought helps you most?
o: "I'll find out which questions I got wrong and practise those."
questions.why: Looking at mistakes turns disappointment into a plan.

questions.q: Your friend Aarav suddenly becomes quiet after his parents' meeting at school. What is the best step?
o: Ask him privately if he wants to talk
Ask him loudly in front of everyone
Ignore him so he doesn't feel awkward
Tease him to cheer him up
questions.why: A private, gentle check-in respects his feelings.

questions.q: You feel angry because your sibling used your phone without asking. What should you do first?
o: Wait until you are calm, then talk about it
Take their things to get even
Tell your parents they broke it
questions.why: Talking when calm makes it more likely you'll be heard.

questions.q: You were not chosen for the school football team. How can you handle it?
o: Feel the disappointment, then ask the coach what to improve
questions.why: It's okay to feel disappointed, and feedback helps you grow.

questions.q: A classmate keeps tapping the desk during a test and you feel irritated. What is the best response?
o: Politely ask them after the test, or tell the teacher
questions.why: Calm, polite action solves the problem without making it bigger.

questions.q: You notice your heart is beating fast before a speech. What is a good way to calm it?
o: Breathe in for four counts and out for six
questions.why: Slow breathing, especially a longer breath out, calms the body.

questions.q: Your best friend tells you a secret that worries you because someone may get hurt. What should you do?
o: Tell a trusted adult, because safety comes first
Keep it secret no matter what
questions.why: When someone's safety is at risk, telling a trusted adult is the right thing.

questions.q: You feel jealous when your sister gets praise for her dance. Which is the healthiest step?
o: Notice the feeling and congratulate her
questions.why: Naming jealousy and still being kind keeps relationships strong.

questions.q: You made a mistake in a group project and the group is upset. What should you say?
o: "I'm sorry, that was my mistake. Here's how I'll fix it."
Stay silent and hope they forget
questions.why: Owning a mistake and offering a fix rebuilds trust.

questions.q: Your friend got a phone and you didn't. You feel left out. What helps most?
o: Talk honestly with your parents about how you feel
questions.why: Sharing your feelings honestly can lead to understanding.

questions.q: A friend shares good news, but you're having a bad day. What's the kind response?
o: Say you're happy for them, and share your day later
Tell them your problem is bigger
questions.why: You can care about others even when you feel low.

questions.q: You are feeling stressed with many homework tasks. What helps first?
o: Make a list and start with the most urgent task
Do all of them at the same time
questions.why: A simple list makes stress feel more manageable.

questions.q: Your classmate cries after losing a match. Others laugh. What should you do?
o: Comfort your classmate and ask the others to stop
questions.why: Standing with someone who is hurting is brave and kind.

questions.q: You feel embarrassed after tripping in front of the class. What helps?
o: Laugh it off kindly and carry on
Hide in the washroom all day
Refuse to come to school tomorrow
questions.why: Everyone trips sometimes. Moving on lightly helps the feeling fade.

questions.q: Your grandmother repeats the same story often. How can you respond kindly?
o: Listen patiently and ask a question about it
questions.why: Patience and interest show respect and love.

questions.q: You disagree with your friend's opinion about a movie. What is a respectful reply?
o: "I see it differently. Here's why I liked it."
Roll your eyes and say nothing
questions.why: You can disagree respectfully by explaining your view.

questions.q: You feel very excited and keep interrupting your teacher. What should you do?
o: Write your ideas down and share them when it's your turn
questions.why: Noting ideas helps you manage excitement and wait for your turn.

questions.q: A friend says, "You never listen to me." How should you respond first?
o: "I'm sorry you feel that way. Tell me more."
questions.why: Listening to feedback first helps you understand the problem.

questions.q: You feel nervous meeting your new class after moving to a new city. What is a good step?
o: Tell them your old school was better
questions.why: Starting small helps nervousness ease.

questions.q: Your younger brother broke your science model. You are furious. What's the best thing to do first?
o: Take a few minutes away to cool down
questions.why: Cooling down first stops you from doing something you'll regret.

questions.q: Your friend didn't invite you to their party. What is a good way to handle the hurt?
o: Ask them calmly if there was a reason
Plan a bigger party and not invite them
questions.why: Asking calmly helps you understand before deciding how to feel.

questions.q: Your coach shouts at the team after a loss. You feel upset. What helps?
o: Listen for the useful advice and stay calm
questions.why: Finding the useful message in criticism helps you improve.

questions.q: You keep thinking about a mistake from last week. What can help you let it go?
o: Learn the lesson from it and forgive yourself
questions.why: Learning from a mistake and moving on is healthy.

questions.q: You see a message in the class group making fun of someone. How do you feel and act?
o: Feel uncomfortable and privately support the person, then tell a teacher
Leave it, it's not your business
questions.why: Supporting the target and telling an adult helps stop bullying.

questions.q: Your parents are arguing and you feel scared. What can you do?
o: Go to a quiet place and later tell a trusted adult how you felt
questions.why: Taking care of yourself and talking to a trusted adult is safe and helpful.

questions.q: You feel proud of your art but a classmate calls it boring. What is a confident response?
o: "Thanks for your view. I enjoyed making it."
questions.why: Confidence means valuing your work even when others disagree.

questions.q: You worry your friend is angry with you. What's the best way to find out?
questions.why: Asking directly clears up worry and misunderstandings.

questions.q: You are frustrated because a game level is too hard. What helps?
o: Take a break and come back with a new strategy
questions.why: Breaks and new strategies help with frustration.

questions.q: You notice a classmate always eats alone. What might they feel and what can you do?
o: They may feel lonely; invite them to join you
They are happy alone, ignore them
Ask why they have no friends in front of everyone
questions.why: Noticing loneliness and including someone can mean a lot.

questions.q: Your teacher picks someone else to lead the assembly. You feel disappointed. What's healthy?
o: Accept it and ask to be considered next time
questions.why: Accepting disappointment and asking for another chance is mature.

questions.q: You feel happy after helping your neighbour carry groceries. Why might that be?
o: Helping others often makes us feel good too
questions.why: Kindness often brings a warm feeling to the helper as well.

questions.q: Your friend is quiet and says "I'm fine" but looks sad. What should you do?
o: Say, "I'm here if you want to talk later."
Force them to tell you right now
Believe them and never ask again
questions.why: Leaving the door open respects their space and shows care.

questions.q: You are upset because you lost your favourite pen. What helps keep things in perspective?
o: Remember it's a small loss and look for it calmly
questions.why: Seeing problems in their real size helps you handle them.

questions.q: You want to speak up in class but feel shy. What is a small first step?
o: Raise your hand to answer one easy question
Ask a friend to always speak for you
questions.why: Small steps build confidence.

questions.q: A classmate accuses you of copying, which you didn't do. How do you respond?
o: Stay calm and show your rough work to the teacher
Shout that they are a liar
questions.why: Calm facts are more convincing than anger.

questions.q: You feel restless after sitting for a long time studying. What helps?
o: Take a short walk or stretch, then return
Keep forcing yourself without a break
questions.why: Short movement breaks refresh your mind.

questions.q: Your friend says your joke hurt them. What should you do?
o: Apologise and avoid that joke in future
Say they can't take a joke
questions.why: What matters is how your words landed, so a sincere apology helps.

questions.q: You did really well in a competition. How can you share it without hurting others?
o: Share it happily and congratulate others too
Make fun of those who lost
questions.why: Celebrating while respecting others keeps friendships strong.

questions.q: Your parents compare you with your cousin's marks. You feel hurt. What can you do?
o: Calmly tell them how the comparison makes you feel
questions.why: Calmly sharing feelings helps parents understand.

questions.q: You feel anxious about a doctor's injection. What helps?
o: Ask the doctor what will happen and breathe slowly
questions.why: Knowing what to expect and breathing slowly reduces fear.

questions.q: You and your friend both wanted to be class monitor. Your friend wins. What do you do?
o: Make the job harder for them
questions.why: Honest congratulations keep the friendship strong.

questions.q: You feel sad when a friend moves to another city. What helps?
questions.why: Staying in touch helps with the sadness of missing someone.

questions.q: You notice you snap at people when you're tired. What's a smart plan?
o: Get enough sleep and pause before replying when tired
questions.why: Knowing your triggers helps you manage your reactions.

questions.q: Your friend made a mistake that cost your team the quiz. What's the kind response?
o: "It's okay, we all make mistakes. Next time!"
Tell the teacher to change teams
questions.why: Kind words help a friend who already feels bad.

questions.q: You feel happy and want to share it. What's a good way?
o: Tell your family about your good day at dinner
Tease those who had a bad day
questions.why: Sharing joy with people close to you doubles the happiness.

questions.q: You realise you have been rude to the canteen uncle. What should you do?
questions.why: Owning up to rudeness shows respect for everyone.

questions.q: A friend shares that their pet died. What's the best response?
o: "I'm so sorry. You must really miss them."
questions.why: Acknowledging the loss shows understanding.

questions.q: You feel nervous when a teacher asks you a question suddenly. What can you do?
o: Take a breath, think, and answer what you know
questions.why: A breath gives your brain time to find the answer.

questions.q: You see your mother looking worried while on the phone. What can you do?
o: Ask gently if she's okay and if you can help
questions.why: Noticing and offering help shows emotional awareness.

questions.q: You get angry when you lose at board games. Which plan helps most?
o: Remind yourself before playing that it's just for fun
Cheat to make sure you win
Throw the board when you lose
questions.why: Setting your mind before a game helps you stay calm.

questions.q: Your friend gets angry and shouts at you. What helps most in the moment?
o: Stay calm and say, "Let's talk when we're both calm."
questions.why: Staying calm stops the argument getting bigger.

questions.q: You are proud that you improved your handwriting. What can you say to yourself?
o: "It's still not perfect, so it doesn't count."
questions.why: Recognising effort builds motivation.

questions.q: A classmate seems nervous before their speech. What can you do?
o: Give them a thumbs up and a smile
questions.why: Encouragement helps nervous people feel supported.

questions.q: You feel bored and irritable during the holidays. What's a good idea?
o: Start a small project like a scrapbook
questions.why: Having a fun goal helps with boredom.

questions.q: You were wrong in an argument with your friend. What should you do?
o: Blame them for making you wrong
questions.why: Admitting you were wrong shows maturity.

questions.q: You feel overwhelmed by exam stress. Who can you talk to?
o: A parent, teacher or school counsellor
Nobody, you must handle it alone
questions.why: Trusted adults can help you manage stress.

questions.q: You feel happy when your team wins, but the other team looks sad. What's a good sport?
questions.why: Good sportsmanship respects everyone's feelings.

questions.q: You realise you've been grumpy all day. What's a good step?
o: Think about why and do something to feel better
questions.why: Understanding why you feel a certain way helps you change it.

questions.q: Your friend is excited about a hobby you find boring. How can you respond?
o: Ask what they enjoy about it
questions.why: Showing interest in what matters to friends builds connection.

questions.q: You feel nervous about your first day in a new sports class. What helps?
o: Remind yourself everyone was new once
questions.why: Remembering that others were new too reduces nerves.

questions.q: You feel annoyed when your friend is always late. What can you do?
o: Tell them kindly how it affects you
questions.why: Telling them honestly and kindly can change the situation.

questions.q: You helped a classmate with homework and they didn't say thanks. What's healthy?
o: Remember you helped because you wanted to, not for thanks
questions.why: Helping because it's right feels good, even without thanks.

questions.q: You feel shy about your new glasses. What helps?
o: Remember lots of people wear glasses and they help you see
questions.why: Seeing changes in a positive way helps confidence.

questions.q: Your friend is upset that you told someone their secret. What should you do?
o: Apologise sincerely and promise to keep secrets in future
questions.why: Trust is rebuilt by sincere apologies and better choices.

questions.q: You notice your hands shaking when you're angry. What does it tell you?
o: Your body is reacting to strong feelings; time to calm down
questions.why: Noticing body signals helps you manage emotions early.

questions.q: You missed your favourite TV show because of a family event. How can you handle it?
o: Watch it later and enjoy the family event
questions.why: Being flexible helps you enjoy the moment.

questions.q: A friend jokes about your height. It hurts. What's a confident response?
o: "I don't find that funny. Please stop."
Cry and never talk to them again
questions.why: Clear, calm words set a healthy boundary.

questions.q: You feel nervous waiting for exam results. What helps most?
o: Keep busy with something you enjoy
questions.why: Staying busy with something enjoyable eases waiting.

questions.q: Your classmate is upset because her drawing was torn. What can you do?
o: Help her tape it and say it still looks great
questions.why: Helping and encouraging shows empathy.

questions.q: You realise you're very angry at your friend over a small thing. What helps?
o: Ask yourself if it will matter in a week
questions.why: Checking the size of a problem helps calm big feelings.

questions.q: You get a lower grade than your friend on a project you worked hard on. Which response shows emotional maturity?
o: Acknowledge the disappointment, then review the feedback for next time
Insist the teacher favours your friend
Downplay your friend's success to others
questions.why: Mature handling means feeling the emotion and still learning from it.

questions.q: Your friend has been short-tempered for days. What's the most helpful approach?
o: Find a quiet moment to ask how they're really doing
Complain about them to the group
questions.why: Irritability can hide stress; a private check-in can help.

questions.q: You notice that you procrastinate when you feel anxious about a task. What's an effective strategy?
o: Break the task into a tiny first step and start for just five minutes
Wait until you feel completely ready
Tell yourself you work best under pressure
questions.why: Small starts reduce the anxiety that fuels procrastination.

questions.q: During a debate, someone mocks your argument. You feel heat rising. What's the best move?
o: Pause, then respond to the point, not the person
Stay silent for the rest of the debate
questions.why: Responding to ideas keeps the debate fair and shows composure.

questions.q: Your sibling is stressed about board exams and snaps at you. What is the most emotionally intelligent response?
o: Recognise it's stress talking and offer support
Snap back and start a fight
Tell your parents to punish them
Ignore them for the whole month
questions.why: Seeing the cause of behaviour helps you respond with empathy.

questions.q: You receive harsh criticism on your writing in front of the class. What's a constructive way forward?
o: Separate the useful feedback from the tone, and use it
Argue with the teacher in class
questions.why: Useful lessons can be taken even from poorly delivered feedback.

questions.q: Your best friend starts dating someone and spends less time with you. You feel left out. What helps?
o: Tell them you miss them and plan time together
questions.why: Honest communication helps friendships adapt to change.

questions.q: You feel pressure to post a perfect life on social media. Which thought is healthiest?
o: Most posts show highlights, not real life
Everyone else really is happier than me
I need more likes to feel good
I should post more to keep up
questions.why: Recognising that social media is filtered protects self-esteem.

questions.q: A friend confides that they feel hopeless and want to disappear. What should you do?
o: Take it seriously, stay with them, and get a trusted adult or helpline involved
Promise to keep it secret no matter what
Change the topic to cheer them up
questions.why: Serious statements about safety need adult help right away.

questions.q: You realise you were wrong in a group decision that went badly. What's the best way to handle it?
o: Own your part openly and suggest how to recover
Let the group believe someone else decided
Defend the choice at all costs
questions.why: Taking responsibility builds trust and helps the team move forward.

questions.q: You feel envious of a classmate's success in a competition. Which response reflects high EQ?
o: Acknowledge the envy privately and use it to set your own goal
questions.why: Envy can point to what you want; using it as motivation is healthy.

questions.q: You are angry with a teacher's decision. What's the best way to raise it?
o: Request a private meeting and explain calmly with reasons
Argue in front of the class
Refuse to do the teacher's work
questions.why: Respectful, private conversations are more effective.

questions.q: You notice your mood dips every Sunday night before school. What helps?
o: Plan something small to look forward to on Monday and prepare early
Stay up late to avoid Monday
questions.why: Planning and preparing can ease anticipatory worry.

questions.q: Your friend shares a problem and you want to fix it immediately. What's often more helpful first?
o: Listen fully and ask what kind of support they want
Give a list of solutions at once
Tell them about your bigger problem
questions.why: People often need to feel heard before they want solutions.

questions.q: Your parent criticises your career choice. You feel hurt. What's a mature step?
o: Ask about their concerns and share your reasons calmly
Shout that they never support you
Give up your choice to avoid conflict
questions.why: Understanding concerns allows a respectful conversation.

questions.q: You keep replaying an awkward moment from a party. What helps?
o: Remind yourself others likely forgot it and move on
questions.why: Most people are focused on themselves, not your awkward moments.

questions.q: A teammate makes a big mistake right before a deadline. What is the emotionally intelligent response?
o: Stay calm, focus on fixing it together
Fix it alone and complain later
Report them to the teacher at once
questions.why: Calm, solution-focused responses help the team recover.

questions.q: You feel burnt out after weeks of study without breaks. What's the healthiest change?
o: Build regular rest, sleep and enjoyable activities into your schedule
questions.why: Rest is part of performing well, not a weakness.

questions.q: You realise a joke you shared online upset someone. What should you do?
o: Explain it was just a joke
Leave it up, it's free speech
questions.why: Taking down hurtful content and apologising shows responsibility.

questions.q: You feel nervous during a job or college interview. Which approach helps most?
o: Treat the nerves as excitement and focus on your prepared stories
questions.why: Reframing nerves as excitement can improve performance.

questions.q: Your friend is grieving a family loss. What's the most supportive thing?
o: Be present, listen, and offer practical help
Avoid them because you don't know what to say
Tell them everything happens for a reason
Encourage them to move on quickly
questions.why: Presence and practical help matter more than perfect words.

questions.q: You lose your temper and say something hurtful to your sibling. What should you do next?
o: Apologise, explain what you felt, and repair the relationship
questions.why: Repairing after conflict strengthens relationships.

questions.q: You notice you feel low whenever you scroll for hours. What's a smart response?
o: Set time limits and notice how you feel after
questions.why: Noticing patterns helps you make healthier choices.

questions.q: A classmate gives you a compliment and you feel awkward. What's a confident response?
o: Simply say "Thank you, that means a lot"
Say "No, I'm not good at that"
Immediately compliment them back to change the topic
questions.why: Accepting compliments graciously builds self-worth.

questions.q: Your group ignores your ideas in a meeting. You feel frustrated. What's effective?
o: Calmly restate your idea with a clear example
Complain to the teacher about each member
questions.why: Clear, calm restating helps ideas get heard.

questions.q: You feel anxious about the future and what career to choose. What helps most?
o: Explore options step by step and talk to mentors
Avoid thinking about it at all
questions.why: Gradual exploration with guidance reduces uncertainty.

questions.q: You see a friend being excluded from a group chat. What can you do?
o: Check in with them and gently raise it with the group
questions.why: Supporting the excluded friend shows empathy and courage.

questions.q: You're happy about your results but your friend didn't do well. How do you balance it?
o: Celebrate quietly and be supportive of your friend
Tell them they should have studied more
questions.why: Sensitivity to others' feelings is key to emotional intelligence.

questions.q: Your coach gives you feedback you disagree with. What's the best response?
o: Ask questions to understand the reasoning, then decide
Pretend to agree and do nothing
questions.why: Seeking to understand before judging is mature.

questions.q: You feel uncomfortable with a group's plan to skip class. What should you do?
o: Politely say no and suggest another plan
Secretly report them without saying anything to them
questions.why: Standing by your values respectfully is a sign of emotional strength.

questions.q: You notice that you get defensive when receiving feedback. What's a helpful habit?
o: Pause and say "Thank you, let me think about that"
Always explain why you were right
questions.why: Pausing helps you respond thoughtfully instead of defensively.

questions.q: Your friend is excited about something you think is a bad idea. What's the best approach?
o: Ask questions and share concerns kindly
Say nothing and watch them fail
Tell others it's a bad idea
questions.why: Respectful questions help friends think without feeling attacked.

questions.q: You feel sad but don't know why. What can help?
o: Write about your feelings or talk to someone you trust
Ignore it and keep busy forever
questions.why: Expressing feelings helps you understand them.

questions.q: After a fight with a close friend, you both stop talking. What's a mature step?
o: Reach out first to talk things through
Wait for them to apologise first
questions.why: Taking the first step shows maturity.

questions.q: You're asked to give a speech at a farewell and feel emotional. What's best?
o: Prepare well and let some emotion show—it's genuine
Joke the whole time to hide feelings
questions.why: Honest emotion can make a speech more meaningful.

questions.q: You failed a school swimming test you had practised for. Which inner voice is most helpful?
o: "I'll practise the parts I missed and retake it."
questions.why: A growth-focused inner voice helps you try again.

questions.q: Your parents seem stressed about money. What can you do?
o: Offer support, avoid unnecessary demands, and ask how you can help
Blame them for not earning more
questions.why: Understanding and support helps the family.

questions.q: You notice a teammate always stays silent in meetings. What's a good approach?
o: Invite their opinion directly but gently
Assume they have nothing to add
questions.why: Inviting quieter voices helps everyone feel valued.

questions.q: You feel angry that your friend didn't support you publicly. What's best?
o: Tell them privately how it made you feel
Call them out on social media
questions.why: Private, honest conversations solve conflicts better.

questions.q: You're preparing for a competitive exam and comparing yourself to others constantly. What helps?
o: Track your own progress against your own past scores
questions.why: Comparing with your own past helps you stay focused and motivated.

questions.q: Someone you admire criticises your work. You feel crushed. What's a healthy reaction?
o: Feel the sting, then look for useful points
questions.why: Strong emotions are normal; learning from feedback is the goal.

questions.q: You become very irritated by a younger cousin's questions. What can help you respond kindly?
o: Remember curiosity is how they learn and answer simply
Tell them to stop being annoying
questions.why: Understanding their perspective helps you be patient.

questions.q: You feel guilty after missing a friend's important event. What's best?
o: Apologise sincerely and ask how it went
questions.why: A sincere apology and genuine interest repair the relationship.

questions.q: You realise you've been short with your family because of exam stress. What helps?
o: Explain that you're stressed and apologise for snapping
Keep it up until exams end
questions.why: Explaining your stress helps family understand and support you.

questions.q: You see a classmate being hard on themselves after a mistake. What's supportive?
o: Remind them that one mistake doesn't define them
Agree that it was a big failure
questions.why: Encouraging self-kindness helps others recover.

questions.q: You feel uncomfortable when a friend makes a hurtful joke about another group. What's a good response?
o: Calmly say you don't think that's funny
Stop being friends without saying why
questions.why: Calmly voicing discomfort can change behaviour.

questions.q: Your friend got into a college you wanted. You feel mixed emotions. What's healthy?
o: Congratulate them and accept your mixed feelings
Hide your feelings and avoid them
questions.why: It's normal to feel both happy and sad; both can be respected.

questions.q: You notice that you often say yes to requests and then feel resentful. What's a healthy change?
o: Learn to politely say no when you can't commit
Say yes but do a poor job
questions.why: Setting boundaries protects your time and relationships.

questions.q: You feel nervous about a difficult conversation with a friend. What helps?
o: Plan what you want to say and choose a calm time
questions.why: Planning helps difficult conversations go better.

questions.q: You receive praise for a group effort as if it were only yours. What's right?
questions.why: Giving credit to others shows integrity and respect.

questions.q: You notice you feel happier after helping at a community event. What can you learn?
o: Contributing to others boosts your own wellbeing
Helping is a waste of time
You should only help for rewards
questions.why: Purpose and helping others are linked to wellbeing.

questions.q: A friend repeatedly cancels plans at the last minute. What's the best approach?
o: Tell them how it affects you and ask what's going on
Cancel on them to teach a lesson
Stop inviting them without a word
questions.why: Open communication may reveal problems and solve the pattern.

questions.q: You're overwhelmed by a breakup or ended friendship. What helps most?
o: Allow yourself to grieve and lean on supportive people
questions.why: Grief after any loss is natural; support helps healing.

questions.q: You notice your teammate is anxious before a match. What's the best support?
o: Remind them of their strengths and the team's plan
Tell them not to mess up
questions.why: Focusing on strengths builds confidence.

questions.q: You feel tempted to retaliate after someone spreads a rumour about you. What's wise?
o: Address it calmly with facts and involve an adult if needed
Spread a worse rumour about them
Get your friends to target them
questions.why: Calm, factual action stops rumours without creating new harm.

questions.q: You find it hard to name your emotions. What can help?
o: Use a feelings list to find more precise words
questions.why: Precise words for feelings make them easier to manage.

questions.q: Your friend shares an achievement but you're struggling. What's an emotionally intelligent response?
o: Celebrate them sincerely, and later share your own struggle with someone
Change the topic to your problems
Tell them it's not that impressive
questions.why: You can hold your own difficulty and still celebrate others.

questions.q: You're asked to mediate between two arguing friends. What's the best first step?
o: Let each person speak without interruption
Take the side of your closest friend
questions.why: Hearing both sides fairly is the first step to resolution.

questions.q: You keep feeling irritated at a classmate for no clear reason. What's wise?
o: Reflect on what triggers you and whether it's about them or you
questions.why: Self-reflection reveals the real cause of strong feelings.

questions.q: You're feeling pressured by your friends to try something unsafe. What's best?
o: Say no firmly and leave if needed
Go along to avoid looking uncool
Make up a lie and do it later
Stay silent and hope it passes
questions.why: Your safety comes before peer pressure.

questions.q: You feel disappointed that a long-planned trip got cancelled. What helps?
o: Acknowledge the disappointment and plan something else to look forward to
questions.why: Naming feelings and refocusing helps you bounce back.

questions.q: You notice a family member seems withdrawn lately. What could you do?
o: Spend time with them and gently ask how they are
Wait for them to come to you
questions.why: Gentle attention can help someone open up.

questions.q: A senior at your articleship firm criticises your audit working papers in front of others. What's the most emotionally intelligent response?
o: Stay composed, note the points, and ask for a short private discussion later
Argue back to defend your work
Complain about the senior to other articles
questions.why: Composure and seeking clarity privately show professionalism.

questions.q: You feel anxious the night before a CA exam paper. What helps most?
o: Do a light revision of key points and sleep on time
Start a new chapter you haven't read
questions.why: Rest and a calm revision improve recall more than last-minute cramming.

questions.q: A client is visibly frustrated about a delayed GST filing. What's the best first step?
o: Acknowledge their frustration and explain the next steps clearly
Blame the client for late documents
Avoid their calls until it's done
Tell them it's not a big deal
questions.why: Acknowledging feelings and offering a clear plan calms a client.

questions.q: Your colleague gets the promotion you wanted. Which response shows emotional maturity?
o: Congratulate them and ask your manager what to develop for next time
Ask for a transfer at once
questions.why: Turning disappointment into a development plan is mature.

questions.q: You notice you get irritated when interrupted during deep work. What's a good strategy?
o: Block focus time on your calendar and communicate it
questions.why: Managing your environment prevents emotional reactions.

questions.q: A junior article asks a question you think is basic. How should you respond?
o: Answer patiently and point them to a good resource
questions.why: Patience with juniors builds trust and a good team.

questions.q: You made an error in a client's tax computation that you found before filing. What's right?
o: Correct it and inform your senior openly
Fix it quietly and say nothing
Leave it, as the amount is small
questions.why: Transparency about errors builds professional trust.

questions.q: You feel overwhelmed by work deadlines and study during articleship. What's a healthy step?
o: Discuss priorities with your principal and plan study blocks
Hide your stress and keep going
questions.why: Open conversations about workload help prevent burnout.

questions.q: A client shouts at you on a call. What's the best response?
o: Stay calm, listen, and say you'll help resolve it
Agree to everything to end the call
questions.why: Staying calm de-escalates the situation.

questions.q: You feel demotivated after failing one group of the CA exam. Which thought helps?
o: "I'll analyse what went wrong and adjust my plan."
questions.why: Analysing failure and adjusting builds resilience.

questions.q: Your team lead praises your work in a meeting. How do you respond?
o: Thank them and credit teammates who helped
Claim it was all your work
questions.why: Sharing credit builds a strong team.

questions.q: A colleague seems upset after a client meeting. What can you do?
o: Check in privately and offer support
Ask about it in front of others
Ignore it, it's not your business
questions.why: Private support shows empathy at work.

questions.q: You disagree with your manager's approach to an audit. What's the best way?
o: Share your view respectfully with reasons, then respect the final decision
Do it your own way secretly
questions.why: Respectful disagreement is professional.

questions.q: You feel nervous presenting to a client's board. What helps?
o: Prepare thoroughly and focus on how the findings help them
Memorise and read without eye contact
questions.why: Preparation and a helpful focus reduce nerves.

questions.q: You notice a fellow article seems isolated and quiet. What's a good step?
o: Invite them to lunch with the team
Point it out in a meeting
questions.why: Inclusion helps people feel part of the team.

questions.q: You get critical feedback in your performance review. What's mature?
o: Thank the reviewer and ask for specific examples
questions.why: Seeking specifics turns feedback into growth.

questions.q: A client tells you about a personal loss while discussing their accounts. What's appropriate?
o: Express sincere sympathy and offer to handle the urgent filings first, within the due dates
Ask for details of the loss
questions.why: Respectful empathy builds client relationships.

questions.q: You realise you're constantly checking work email late at night. What's a healthy change?
o: Set a cut-off time for work email
questions.why: Boundaries protect your rest and long-term performance.

questions.q: Your senior takes credit for your idea in a meeting. What's the best approach?
o: Talk to them privately and calmly about it
questions.why: A calm, private talk is professional and effective.

questions.q: You feel jealous of a batchmate who cleared CA in the first attempt. What helps?
o: Use their journey as inspiration and focus on your own plan
questions.why: Turning envy into inspiration helps your own progress.

questions.q: You have to tell a client that their expected tax refund will be lower. How should you communicate?
o: Explain the reasons clearly and calmly, with what can be done next
Send a short email without explanation
questions.why: Clear, honest communication with next steps respects the client.

questions.q: A teammate is struggling with a new accounting software. What should you do?
o: Offer to show them the key steps
Do the work for them every time
questions.why: Helping colleagues learn builds team strength.

questions.q: You feel bored with repetitive vouching work. What's a healthy approach?
o: Look for patterns and learning in the work, and ask for varied tasks
questions.why: Finding meaning and asking for variety keeps you engaged.

questions.q: Your manager is stressed and short with the team. What's the emotionally intelligent response?
o: Stay calm, deliver your work, and offer help where possible
questions.why: Understanding stress helps you respond calmly.

questions.q: You feel nervous about your first day of articleship. What's a good mindset?
o: Everyone starts new; focus on learning and asking good questions
questions.why: A learning mindset eases first-day nerves.

questions.q: You made a promise to a client you can't keep. What's best?
o: Inform them early, apologise, and offer an alternative
questions.why: Early honesty protects trust.

questions.q: A colleague is upset about their workload and vents to you. What's helpful?
o: Listen and help them think of who to talk to about it
questions.why: Listening and guiding toward solutions is supportive.

questions.q: You feel frustrated that a client keeps changing requirements. What's mature?
o: Calmly document the changes and agree on timelines
questions.why: Clear documentation keeps things professional and fair.

questions.q: You notice your confidence drops before each mock test. What helps?
o: Remind yourself of past progress and treat mocks as practice
questions.why: Mocks are for learning; remembering progress builds confidence.

questions.q: A junior makes a mistake that delays your report. What's the best response?
o: Help fix it and explain how to avoid it next time
Redo all their work without telling them
questions.why: Teaching from mistakes builds better juniors.

questions.q: You feel uneasy about an instruction that seems unethical. What's right?
o: Raise your concern with your senior or principal and follow professional ethics
Ignore it and hope for the best
questions.why: Professional ethics must come first; raising concerns is the right step.

questions.q: Your colleague keeps interrupting you in meetings. What's the best approach?
o: Calmly say "Let me finish, then I'd love your view"
questions.why: Calm, direct words protect your voice in meetings.

questions.q: You notice a client's staff member is nervous during the audit. What can help?
o: Explain the process and reassure them it's routine
Ask questions in a harsh tone
questions.why: Reassurance helps people cooperate during audits.

questions.q: You feel low after a long day of mistakes. What helps?
o: Reflect briefly, note one lesson, and rest
Keep working late to make up
questions.why: Short reflection and rest help you start fresh.

questions.q: Your friend from coaching is anxious about results day. What's supportive?
o: Stay with them and remind them that one result doesn't define them
Talk only about your own chances
questions.why: Calm support and perspective help anxious friends.

questions.q: You are offered constructive advice by a peer you don't like. What's mature?
o: Judge the advice on its merits, not the person
Reject it because of who said it
questions.why: Good advice is useful whoever it comes from.

questions.q: You need to say no to an extra task because you're overloaded. How?
o: Explain your current workload and suggest when you could help
questions.why: A clear, polite no with an alternative is professional.

questions.q: Your manager is unhappy about a missed deadline. What's best?
o: Own it, explain briefly, and present a recovery plan
questions.why: Ownership with a plan shows accountability.

questions.q: You sense tension between two team members. What can you do?
o: Encourage them to talk directly, and stay neutral
questions.why: Encouraging direct communication helps resolve conflicts.

questions.q: You feel proud after cracking a complex reconciliation. What's healthy?
o: Acknowledge your effort and share the method with the team
questions.why: Celebrating progress and sharing knowledge builds you and the team.

questions.q: You notice you feel tense when your phone shows a client's name. What's a good step?
o: Notice the tension, breathe, and answer with a plan in mind
Answer and speak quickly to finish
questions.why: Awareness and preparation reduce tension.

questions.q: A client thanks you warmly for your help. How can you respond?
o: Thank them and say you're glad it helped
questions.why: Graciously accepting thanks builds the relationship.

questions.q: Your study partner falls behind and feels bad. What's supportive?
o: Offer to review a topic together
questions.why: Supporting peers helps both learn better.

questions.q: You realise you've been rude to the office peon when stressed. What should you do?
o: Apologise and treat everyone with respect
questions.why: Respect for everyone at work is a sign of good character.

questions.q: Your principal gives you a challenging new assignment. You feel nervous. What helps?
o: See it as trust in you and ask for guidance where needed
questions.why: Seeing challenges as trust builds confidence.

questions.q: You receive a rude email from a client. What's best?
o: Wait before replying, then respond politely and factually
questions.why: Pausing before replying prevents regret.

questions.q: You feel isolated working remotely during an audit. What helps?
o: Schedule quick check-ins with your team
questions.why: Regular check-ins maintain connection.

questions.q: You notice your colleague is not eating lunch and seems stressed. What's kind?
o: Invite them for lunch and ask if they're okay
Report it to the manager without speaking to them
questions.why: A small kind gesture can help someone open up.

questions.q: You're asked to present a mistake you made to the team as a learning example. You feel embarrassed. What's healthy?
o: Share it openly, focusing on the lesson
Blame someone else in the presentation
Make it sound smaller than it was
questions.why: Openly sharing lessons builds a learning culture and your credibility.

questions.q: You are chosen as class captain and a friend who wanted it is cold towards you. What's the wisest step?
o: Acknowledge their disappointment privately and ask for their help
Use your new role to give them fewer duties
Ignore the coldness and hope it fades
questions.why: Recognising their feelings and including them can restore the friendship.

questions.q: Your hands sweat and your mind goes blank in a maths exam. What helps you recover?
o: Pause, take a few slow breaths, and start with a question you know
Stare at the hardest question until it makes sense
questions.why: Calming the body and starting with an easy win restarts your thinking.

questions.q: A friend keeps making plans without asking you and you feel taken for granted. What's best?
o: Tell them calmly that you'd like to be asked first
Quietly drop out of every plan
Make plans that leave them out
Post a hint about it online
questions.why: Calm, direct feedback is the clearest way to change a pattern.

questions.q: You realise you're laughing along with a group that's teasing a younger student. What should you do?
o: Stop laughing, and check on the student afterwards
Laugh harder so no one notices
Join in with your own joke
questions.why: Noticing your part and changing it shows real emotional strength.

questions.q: Your parents are proud of a mark you're unhappy with. How do you handle the mixed feelings?
o: Thank them, and quietly set your own goal for next time
Pretend you're happy and say nothing to yourself
questions.why: You can accept their pride and still hold your own goal.

questions.q: You feel a sudden wave of anger when a stranger cuts the queue. What's the best response?
o: Calmly point out the queue and let it go if they refuse
Push them out of the line
Stew about it for the rest of the day
questions.why: A calm word is enough; carrying the anger only hurts you.

questions.q: Your friend apologises for something that really hurt you, but you're still upset. What's honest and kind?
o: Thank them, and say you need a little time to feel okay again
Bring it up in every argument
questions.why: Accepting an apology while being honest about your feelings is healthy.

questions.q: A new student mispronounces words and some classmates giggle. What can you do?
o: Talk to the new student normally and change the topic for the gigglers
Giggle too so you fit in
Correct them loudly in front of everyone
Ignore it, it's not your problem
questions.why: Quiet kindness helps a newcomer feel safe and makes teasing less fun.

questions.q: You must give an article junior negative feedback on a sloppy file. What's the best way?
o: Give specific points in private and agree on how to improve
Point out the mistakes in front of the team
Say nothing and fix it yourself
Send a one-line "this is wrong" message
questions.why: Specific, private feedback helps juniors improve without losing confidence.
